title: The Entire History of Ethiopia
summary: How Ethiopia's rulers built unity against foreign conquest while struggling over power inside the state.

scenes.narration: Italy expects a conquest. Instead, its army is marching toward a catastrophe. It's eighteen ninety-six, and General Baratieri has ordered his columns into the hills around Adwa. They're supposed to support each other. In the darkness, they lose contact. Now they're separate targets. Ahead of them, Emperor Menelik's much larger Ethiopian army is waiting.

Menelik hasn't just assembled soldiers. He's brought rivals into the same camp, alongside Empress Taytu. At Adwa, that coalition will defeat a European invader. But getting people to fight together is one thing. Getting them to agree about who rules afterward is another. That problem begins long before Italy arrives, in a kingdom whose power travels with its merchants.

Nearly two thousand years earlier, Aksum sits between the African highlands and the Red Sea. Goods move toward Arabia and the Indian Ocean. The rulers take their share, and trade helps pay for a powerful kingdom. By the third century, they mint their own coins. Royal power can now travel in somebody else's pocket.

In the fourth century, King Ezana adopts Christianity. That connects Aksum to other Christian powers and gives the monarchy a lasting religious identity. A king can now claim more than control of an army or a trading route. His position belongs within a sacred order. That's useful when somebody else starts wondering whether they'd make a better king.

But wealth follows trade, and trade routes don't promise to stay put. As Aksum declines, political power shifts deeper into the highlands. Under the Zagwe dynasty, churches are carved into the rock at Lalibela. They serve worshippers and display royal ambition on an extraordinary scale. The overseas trading network has faded. The monarchy is finding another way to make its power visible.

In twelve seventy, Yekuno Amlak overthrows the Zagwe. Taking the throne is the immediate job. Explaining why he deserves it comes next. The dynasty that follows claims descent from King Solomon and the Queen of Sheba. That's a claim to authority, not a family tree historians can simply confirm. Military success gets the new rulers into power. A very impressive ancestry helps justify keeping it.

An impressive ancestry can't stop an invading army. In the sixteenth century, Ahmed of Adal's campaigns devastate the Christian kingdom. Portuguese military help contributes to his defeat in fifteen forty-three. The monarchy survives, but a defeated enemy doesn't repair ruined communities or restore lost resources. Local rulers still have their own troops and ambitions. Winning this war leaves the next ruler with a battered country to hold together.

Emperor Fasilides establishes a capital at Gondar in the sixteen-thirties. Its castles give royal power a permanent address. Later, the Era of the Princes reverses that image. Emperors keep their titles while regional warlords control much of the actual power. The crown is still there. The ability to make the provinces obey often isn't. For an ambitious ruler, reunification is both an opportunity and a fight.

In the nineteenth century, Tewodros the second tries to pull that power back to the center. He dies before finishing the job. Yohannes the fourth then faces pressure and invasions from neighboring powers, including Egypt and the Mahdist state. Defending the country requires cooperation. Building a stronger throne means asking regional rulers to surrender some of their independence. Those aren't always compatible requests.

Menelik, the king of Shewa, approaches the problem with diplomacy, conquest and imported rifles. His expansion helps shape modern Ethiopia's territory and gives his state more resources. From the court, it looks like a stronger country taking shape. For communities conquered in the south, it can mean lost land, imposed obligations and rule by outsiders. A foreign invasion won't erase them.

scenes.narration: Then Italy tries to turn an agreement into control. The Treaty of Wuchale, signed in eighteen eighty-nine, reads differently in Italian and Amharic. In the Amharic version, Ethiopia could use Italy for foreign diplomacy. In the Italian version, it had to. Optional in one language. Compulsory in the other. Italy claims a protectorate. Menelik rejects it, and Taytu helps organize resistance. The argument has moved beyond wording. Who gets to speak for Ethiopia?

Now we're back at Adwa. Menelik and Taytu have helped bring regional leaders and their armies together. Imported weapons, preparation and that coalition matter as much as Italy's mistakes. When Baratieri's brigades become separated, they face a much larger Ethiopian force without the coordination they need. The invasion collapses. The victory isn't a lucky exception to European power. Ethiopian leaders have organized the means to defeat it.

Italy recognizes Ethiopian independence. Adwa shows that conquest can be resisted, and the victory becomes a national symbol. Yet people living inside Menelik's expanding empire haven't all gained the same freedoms. Communities brought under his rule still have grievances over land and authority. Making its government acceptable to everyone at home remains a different, unfinished task.

scenes.asset_search_term: 1935 Italian invasion Ethiopia aircraft mustard gas
scenes.narration: Four decades later, Italy comes back. Mussolini wants an empire and revenge for Adwa. This invasion brings aircraft and chemical weapons. Italian forces use mustard gas despite international prohibitions. Ethiopian armies resist, but determination can't remove that technological disadvantage. The balance has changed brutally. A country that defeated one invasion now faces an enemy prepared to wage a different kind of war.

In nineteen thirty-six, Italian troops enter Addis Ababa. Haile Selassie goes into exile and appeals to the League of Nations. The international response doesn't give him the protection he needs. Inside Ethiopia, resistance continues. Capturing the capital lets Italy announce a conquest. It doesn't make the countryside obedient. Beyond the garrisons, Ethiopian fighters keep challenging an occupation that is far less settled than its conquerors want to claim.

The Second World War changes the balance again. In nineteen forty-one, Ethiopian patriots and British-led forces defeat Italian rule. Haile Selassie returns, and the monarchy is restored. An emperor who left in exile is back in his capital. But rebuilding the state means deciding where its power will sit. The throne returns. Its problems return with it.

By nineteen seventy-four, hardship and anger reach the army. At Nagelle, soldiers arrest their officers over shortages of food and water. When a general arrives to negotiate, they make him eat and drink what they've been given. Protests spread. A military committee called the Derg removes Haile Selassie. The officers promise transformation. They show much less interest in letting opponents decide what that should mean.

Mengistu Haile Mariam emerges as the dominant figure. During the Red Terror, the regime imprisons and kills opponents. A political disagreement can become a death sentence. Revolutionary socialism has replaced the language of monarchy, but the government still demands obedience. For communities resisting central control, the danger is immediate. Challenging the state can mean being treated as an enemy to be eliminated, rather than a citizen to be heard.

Then war and drought combine with coercive government policies to deepen the famine of the nineteen-eighties. This isn't explained by missing rain alone. Fighting disrupts livelihoods and access to food. State decisions make the suffering worse. People face hunger while roads, supplies and their movements are caught up in a war. The regime promises transformation. Millions are struggling to survive.

In nineteen ninety-one, rebel forces enter Addis Ababa. The Derg falls. After years of military rule and civil war, a new leadership holds the capital. But governing the provinces will require more than replacing the people at the top. Communities want security and recognition. They don't all trust the same rulers to provide them. The next settlement has to address that distrust.

Eritrea votes for independence in nineteen ninety-three. Within Ethiopia, the EPRDF builds a federal system organized largely around ethnic and linguistic regions. Different peoples now have a recognized place in the structure of the state. But boundaries also raise practical questions. Who controls disputed land? Who represents people living on the other side of a regional line? And when a region and the center disagree, whose decision wins?

Abiy Ahmed takes office in twenty eighteen, promising reform. The following year, he brings much of the ruling coalition into the new Prosperity Party. The TPLF refuses to join. A reorganization presented as national renewal also threatens an established balance of power. What looks like a stronger common government to its supporters can look like lost influence and greater central control to its opponents. The disagreement hardens.

In November twenty twenty, the confrontation becomes the Tigray War. Fighting between federal and regional forces grows into a devastating conflict. Civilians face killing, displacement and hunger. Decisions about party organization, regional authority and military power now determine whether families can remain in their homes or find food. The costs fall far beyond the people making those decisions. Another struggle over government has become a struggle to survive.

An African Union-brokered agreement in Pretoria brings a cessation of hostilities in November twenty twenty-two. It's a crucial opening, with grievances still unresolved. At Adwa, Ethiopia's leaders found a way to unite against an invader. The country survived, but the bargain remained: how much power should its rulers hold? Defending a country could bring rivals together. Sharing a country would require them to keep negotiating.
